lead: Earthing (some syllabi say grounding) is a deliberate low-resistance connection from exposed metal and from the supply neutral point to the soil. It exists so a live-to-metal fault sends a large current back to the source and blows the fuse or trips the MCB. It also gives lightning and surge currents a path to earth. You meet it at every three-pin socket, water pump, inverter body and distribution transformer. The earth connection must be real, not the neutral wire.
prereq: You need: Chapter 6.7 for live, neutral and earth wiring; Chapter 6.2 for the megger; and Ohm's law from Unit 1, DC Circuits and Network Theorems.

blocks.text: Earthing is a safety connection. The exposed metal case of a fan, washing machine or inverter is normally not live. If insulation fails, the live wire touches the case. Without earthing, the case stays at 230 V. A person who touches it and stands on a wet floor completes a path through the body to earth. With earthing, the case is wired to an earth electrode buried in soil. The fault current gets a low-resistance path back to the supply. The current becomes large, so the fuse or MCB trips and removes the supply. The danger lasts for a short time. When there is no fault, the metal case sits at earth potential.

Earthing also holds metalwork at a steady reference potential. It gives lightning and switching surges a path to soil instead of through equipment. It stabilises the voltage of a system whose neutral is earthed at the transformer. Safety of persons is the first need; protection of equipment is the second. In Indian homes, the third pin of a 230 V socket is the earth pin. It must go to a real earth pit, never to the neutral.

An earth electrode is the metal part buried in soil. The earth wire joins it to the equipment. The choice depends on soil resistivity, fault current and space. Plate and pipe electrodes are common in homes; mesh is for high-current sites. Common types are listed below.

blocks.text: A plate electrode uses a copper or GI plate in a pit filled with charcoal and salt. A pipe electrode is a GI pipe driven vertically into the ground. A rod electrode is a copper-bonded steel rod, often driven deep. A strip electrode is a GI or copper strip laid in a trench. A mesh electrode is a grid of rods and strips, used where the current is large. Chemical or maintenance-free earthing surrounds the electrode with a backfill such as bentonite, which holds moisture, or graphite, which is conductive. The bentonite backfill holds moisture and keeps the earth resistance stable in dry soil.

The fault path is a loop. It runs from the live wire, through the fault, into the metal body, along the earth wire, into the earth electrode, through the soil, and back to the earthed neutral of the source. The earth wire and electrode must have low resistance.
Let R_e be the total resistance of this earth path in ohms. Let V be the supply voltage to earth in volts. The fault current is:

blocks.where: I_f is the fault current in amperes; V is the supply voltage to earth in volts; R_e is the total earth path resistance in ohms, including the earth wire, electrode and soil return.

blocks.text: For a 230 V supply and R_e = 5 Ω, I_f = 230 / 5 = 46 A. A 16 A MCB sees 46 A as an overcurrent above its rating and trips. If R_e is 100 Ω, I_f is only 2.3 A. A 16 A MCB may not trip, and the metal body stays live. Touch voltage is the voltage a person feels between the metal body and the ground. A low R_e makes the fault current large, so the trip is fast. When the fault itself has some resistance, a low R_e also keeps the touch voltage lower. The earth connection does not absorb current. It provides a return path.

Earth resistance is measured with an earth tester. A three-terminal tester passes a current through the electrode and a current probe, and measures the voltage between the electrode and a potential probe. A clamp-on earth tester measures the earth resistance without disconnecting the electrode. A megger-type instrument is used in some tests. Measure in dry weather, because dry soil gives the worst value. The exact limit comes from the local wiring rule; domestic pits are usually kept to a few ohms or less.

items: Do keep the earth wire joints tight and clean.
Do water the earth pit in summer, if it is a conventional pit.
Do test the earth resistance at fixed intervals.
Do not use the neutral wire as earth. Neutral carries load current and can be at a voltage.
Do not disconnect the earth wire to stop nuisance tripping. Find the fault instead.
Do not use a plastic pipe or a painted metal part as an electrode.

examples.question: A 230 V metal-bodied appliance has a fault from live to body. The earth wire and electrode have a total resistance of 5 Ω. Find the fault current. Will a 16 A MCB see this as a large fault? Take the supply voltage to earth as 230 V.
steps: Write the data: V = 230 V, R_e = 5 Ω.
Compare with the MCB rating: 46 A > 16 A. The ratio is 46/16 = 2.875, so the current is well above the rating.
The MCB sees this as an overcurrent and trips, clearing the fault.
examples.answer: The fault current is 46 A, and yes, the 16 A MCB sees it as a large fault and trips.

traps: Earthing is not a current absorber. It is a low-resistance return path that makes the fuse or MCB trip.
A high earth resistance lowers the fault current. The MCB may not trip, so an RCCB is added for shock protection.
Never use neutral as earth. Neutral carries load current, so its voltage is not zero.
Do not confuse earth resistance with insulation resistance. The megger checks insulation; an earth tester checks the electrode.
In I_f = V/R_e, use R_e in ohms, not kΩ. A 5 kΩ earth path gives only 0.046 A, not 46 A.

quiz.a: Earthing is a deliberate connection from exposed metal or a supply neutral point to the soil through an electrode, to give fault current a low-resistance return path.

quiz.q: Name four types of earth electrode.
quiz.a: Plate, pipe, rod and strip. Mesh and chemical electrodes are also used.

quiz.q: Why does a low earth resistance make a fuse or MCB trip faster?
quiz.a: It makes I_f = V/R_e large. The overcurrent device sees a current above its trip threshold and clears the fault quickly.

quiz.q: A 230 V supply has R_e = 10 Ω. Find I_f. Will a 20 A MCB trip?
quiz.a: I_f = 230/10 = 23 A. 23 A is only slightly above the 20 A rating, so the MCB may not trip quickly. The metal body would stay live for a long time. An RCCB is needed for shock protection.

quiz.q: Why is the neutral wire not a safe earth?
quiz.a: Neutral carries load current and has a voltage drop. It can rise above earth potential. Using it as earth puts the metal body at that voltage.

quiz.q: An earth path has R_e = 100 Ω at 230 V. I_f = 2.3 A. A 16 A MCB does not trip. Explain the danger and the fix.
quiz.a: The metal body stays at a dangerous touch voltage; a person touching it could receive a lethal shock. Add an RCCB/ELCB and improve the earth electrode to lower R_e; the RCCB trips on small earth leakage.

quiz.q: If R_e doubles, what happens to I_f?
quiz.a: I_f halves, because I_f is inversely proportional to R_e.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, substation earthing uses mesh grids designed for step and touch voltage limits. Lightning protection uses separate down conductors and earth terminations. Chemical earthing and remote earth monitors are common in telecom and solar plants. Search next for soil resistivity test, fall of potential test, substation grounding design and RCCB earth leakage.
